# A 90% ECG threshold does not hold at another hospital or in another care setting

Ruben Abbou

PTB-XL · SPH · ACS-ECG · EchoNext · {{d.inf_scored}} tracings scored across three corpora for infarction, and {{d.echo_cohorts}} EchoNext ECGs for structural heart disease · draft of 5 October 2026

## Abstract

An ECG model scores each recording, and a cut-off on the score, the threshold, decides who is called ill; it is typically set to catch 90% of the ill. A hospital adopting the model inherits that cut-off and sees one accuracy score, the AUROC, which does not say how many ill patients that cut-off catches and can look fine while patients are missed.

Cut-offs were moved unchanged to new patients: myocardial infarction, from PTB-XL (Germany) to hospitals in Shandong and Chongqing; sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, left and right bundle-branch block and first-degree atrioventricular block, across five public collections; structural heart disease, from Columbia inpatients to outpatients. Three ways of answering were compared: one cut-off saying yes or no to everyone, and two adding a grey zone where the patient is referred to a doctor (conformal prediction), placed so that 90% of all patients counted together, or 90% of the ill and 90% of the healthy counted separately, get no wrong answer.

Counted together, the 90% hid the ill: at PTB-XL {{s.none.ptbxl.all}} of patients got no wrong answer, but {{s.none.ptbxl.mi}} of infarctions were caught (flagged or referred). Counted separately, 90% of the ill were caught where the cut-offs were set; moved, they caught {{s.mondrian.acs.mi}} of infarctions at Chongqing, {{s.mondrian.sph.mi}} at Shandong, {{rot.mondrian.away.diagnosis}} for the five other diagnoses, and {{resnet_sens_out}} of ill outpatients against {{resnet_sens_in}} of inpatients, while the AUROC barely changed. The share referred to a doctor, visible without knowing diagnoses, fell as more ill patients were missed.

A moved cut-off did not keep its 90%. Reset on a hundred local ECGs with known diagnoses, infarctions caught at Chongqing rose to {{ts.mondrian.recalibrated.100}}, ill outpatients caught to {{ladder_low}}–{{ladder_high}} on average. A site should count how many of its ill patients each cut-off catches, and reset it on about a hundred ECGs.

## 1. Introduction

A cut-off set to catch 90% of the ill at one hospital may catch fewer at another, and the accuracy score a hospital is shown does not reveal it. This section sets out why, and what no study had measured.

An ECG model does not answer yes or no by itself. It gives each tracing, one recorded ECG, a score between 0 and 1, and a threshold, a cut-off on that score, turns the score into an answer: above it, the model calls the disease present. The cut-off is chosen on patients whose diagnoses are known, usually so that it catches a target share of the ill, such as 90%: a sensitivity of 90%. Choosing the cut-off is called calibration, and the patients it is chosen on are the calibration patients. The 90% is a fact about those patients. At a hospital whose patients differ in how common or how severe the disease is, in their recording machines, or in how diagnoses are written down, the same cut-off can catch a different share, and a yes-or-no answer gives no sign that this has happened.

What a receiving hospital is usually shown is the AUROC, the usual single accuracy score: the chance that a randomly chosen ill patient scores higher than a randomly chosen healthy one. It does not say how many ill patients a given cut-off catches. Two studies of one ECG model for a weak heart pump (low ejection fraction) show what follows. In a Russian population study of 4,277 adults, used at the cut-off of its original study, the model kept an AUROC of 0.82 and caught 26.9% of the patients with a weak pump [19]. At four US sites, with a cut-off fixed in advance, it caught 84.5% of them and correctly cleared 83.6% of the others [20]. Whether a cut-off holds at a new site has to be measured each time.

Conformal prediction, a standard statistical method, adds a third answer. Instead of one cut-off it sets two. A patient scoring above the upper one is called ill, below the lower one healthy, and between them, in a grey zone, gets no machine answer: the patient is referred to a doctor, who reads the ECG. A referred patient is not missed, since a doctor sees the ECG, so this study counts an ill patient as caught when the model either flags or refers them, and missed when it calls them healthy. Over all patients, the share given no wrong answer counts those who got the right answer or were referred; statisticians call this share the coverage. The method guarantees the share asked for, say 90%, provided the cut-offs are set on patients the model was not trained on, and provided the patients who will be answered resemble those patients [1]. A change of hospital is exactly what breaks the second condition.

The guarantee has a second limit: it holds for all patients counted together. When the ill are few, 90% over everyone can hide a much lower share among the ill, because the healthy majority makes up most of the count. Setting the two cut-offs for all patients counted together is called pooled calibration. The alternative counts the ill and the healthy separately. The lower cut-off, below which a patient is called healthy, is placed at the score that 90% of the ill calibration patients exceed; the upper cut-off, above which a patient is called ill, at the score that 90% of the healthy calibration patients stay below. This is per-diagnosis calibration; its technical names are class-conditional and Mondrian conformal prediction, and the figures below use the first. It guarantees 90% among the ill and 90% among the healthy, whatever the share of ill patients [2]. The reason is simple: the cut-off for the ill is placed by looking only at ill patients' scores, so whether the ill are a few or half of the patients does not move it [2,4]. If the share of the ill caught still falls after a move, the ill patients themselves score differently.

Earlier work has shown pooled calibration failing the ill where the cut-offs were set, and per-diagnosis calibration repairing it: on skin lesions, where melanomas were under-caught [12]; in drug screening and across fifteen tabular datasets [5,6]; in intensive-care rhythm detection from the pulse oximeter [14]; and on the ECG, for infarction on PTB-XL, by El Allam and Hamlich [15]. None of these moved the cut-offs to another site. Appendix J gives their figures.

For structural heart disease the move that matters stays inside one hospital. A model that detects it from the ECG learns from patients who had an echocardiogram, mostly inpatients, and a screening programme would run it on outpatients. EchoNext, trained on more than a million ECGs from eight New York hospitals, is the reference model for that task, and both of its papers find its AUROC about the same in every care setting [17,18]. Neither reports what a cut-off fixed in one setting catches in another. At another hospital the model's AUROC fell [21], and in a community cohort aged 65 to 85 it fell too, which its authors attribute to milder disease [22].

No study measures, for the ECG, how many of the ill a cut-off catches after it has been carried to other patients without being reset; none sets a single cut-off beside the conformal ones in the terms a clinician uses, and none reports how many patients each option refers. Searches of the ECG literature on 2 and 4 September 2026, repeated on 8 September across PubMed, arXiv, Crossref, OpenAlex, Google Scholar and OpenReview, found none. This study asks one question twice: when a cut-off set to catch 90% at one place is used at another, how many of the ill does it catch, for each diagnosis, and does anything a site can see without knowing the diagnoses show the change? The first test moves infarction cut-offs between hospitals, from PTB-XL to Shandong and Chongqing, and widens that to five collections taking turns at setting cut-offs for five other diagnoses. The second keeps the hospital and moves structural heart disease cut-offs from Columbia's inpatients to its outpatients. The two differ in one useful way: at Chongqing what counts as an infarction changes along with the patients, while at Columbia the definition of the disease stays the same and only the patients change. Every technique applied here is established; the study adds the measurement.

## 2. Methods

ECGs with known diagnoses were split into two groups: on the first the cut-offs were set, on the second they were used unchanged, and the ill patients caught were counted. No model was retrained for the move.

### 2.1 Two moves and their data

For infarction, three public collections of ECGs (corpora) were used. The site where the cut-offs are set is called the source, and a site that receives them unchanged the target. Cut-offs were set on PTB-XL. The two Chinese hospitals received them, and the cut-offs were set without looking at any diagnosis from either hospital. Appendix A accounts for every record.

| Dataset | Country, years | Tracings scored | Share with infarction | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PTB-XL [9] | Germany, 1989–96 | {{inf.ptbxl_n}} | {{inf.ptbxl_prevalence}} | source |
| SPH, Shandong [10] | China, 2019–20 | {{inf.sph_n}} | {{inf.sph_prevalence}} | target |
| ACS-ECG, Chongqing [11] | China, 2015–24 | {{inf.acs_n}} | {{inf.acs_prevalence}} | target |

The three collections define infarction differently. At Chongqing a tracing counts as infarction when the discharge diagnosis names an acute myocardial infarction, in a cohort whose every patient underwent coronary angiography; PTB-XL records what the ECG shows, mostly older infarct patterns. Shandong codes infarction as acute, recent or old, and {{d.sph_old}} of its infarctions are old, so its definition sits closer to PTB-XL's, though the remaining {{d.sph_not_old}} are acute, recent or unspecified. The Shandong move therefore changes mainly how common infarction is, while the Chongqing move also changes what counts as an infarction.

For structural heart disease, EchoNext v1.1.1 holds {{records}} ECGs from Columbia, each recorded within a year before a transthoracic echocardiogram. The diagnosis studied is moderate or worse structural heart disease on that echocardiogram, a composite of eleven findings [18]. EchoNext comes divided into three parts: one to train models on, one to set cut-offs on, and one kept for testing. The cut-offs were set on the {{calibration_ecgs}} inpatients of the second part and used unchanged on the third, which holds {{outpatient_ecgs}} outpatients beside emergency and inpatient ECGs. Each patient contributes one ECG and belongs to one part only.

| Cohort | ECGs, one per patient | Structural heart disease | Ejection fraction 45% or less | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inpatients, part for setting cut-offs | {{calibration_ecgs}} | {{prevalence_in}} | {{d.lvef_in}} | sets the cut-offs |
| Inpatients, test part | {{d.test_inpatient_n}} | {{d.test_inpatient_prev}} | {{d.test_inpatient_lvef}} | receives them, same setting |
| Emergency, test part | {{d.test_emergency_n}} | {{d.test_emergency_prev}} | {{d.test_emergency_lvef}} | receives them |
| Outpatients, test part | {{outpatient_ecgs}} | {{prevalence_out}} | {{d.lvef_out}} | receives them |

Unlike infarction, the diagnosis does not change between these cohorts: every one is read from echocardiograms at the same hospital under the same definitions, so what changes is how many patients are ill and which patients they are.

### 2.2 Models

For infarction, a standard deep-learning network for ECGs (a ResNet) was trained on PTB-XL. PTB-XL is distributed in ten numbered parts: the network learned on parts 1 to 8, part 9 decided when to stop training, and part 10 was kept for testing, where the network's AUROC for infarction is {{inf.baseline_auroc}} (95% confidence interval {{inf.baseline_low}} to {{inf.baseline_high}}). The network was then left unchanged, so every option below works on the same scores and any difference between options comes from where the cut-offs sit. Appendix B describes it.

For structural heart disease, four models scored every ECG. The study's own ResNet, trained on EchoNext's training part, reaches an AUROC of {{ea.resnet.test}} on the test part. The published EchoNext mini-model, run as its authors released it, reaches {{mini_auroc_test}}, close to the 82.0% they report [18]. ECGFounder, a model trained beforehand on more than ten million ECGs from another hospital [24], was used as released, with only a small final step fitted on EchoNext's training part; it reaches {{ea.ecgfounder.test}}. The fourth is the study's ResNet with no training at all, its internal settings left at random, given the same small final step: it shows what a model achieves without learning anything from ECGs, so a useful model has to do better. It reaches {{ea.random_init.test}}. Appendix C gives how each was run.

### 2.3 Three ways of answering a patient

Each model gives every ECG a score, and the scores never change; the three options differ only in where they place the cut-offs and in what they do with a patient whose score falls near them.

The first option, a single cut-off, answers yes or no for every patient. It is placed so that 90% of the ill calibration patients score above it, a sensitivity of 90%, and stands for current practice.

The second and third options are the two forms of conformal prediction described in section 1. Each sets two cut-offs and refers every patient whose score falls between them to a doctor. The second, pooled calibration, places both cut-offs so that 90% of all calibration patients, ill and healthy counted together, get no wrong answer. The third, per-diagnosis calibration, places the lower cut-off so that 90% of the ill calibration patients are not called healthy, and the upper cut-off so that 90% of the healthy are not called ill. Counting all patients together or each diagnosis separately is the only difference between the second and third options.

The single cut-off and the per-diagnosis option catch exactly the same ill patients. Both are placed at the score that 90% of the ill calibration patients exceed: the single cut-off there, and the per-diagnosis option's lower cut-off there too. What the per-diagnosis option adds is its upper cut-off, which turns some healthy patients the single cut-off would have flagged into referrals.

A fourth option, run for infarction and for the five collections, starts from pooled calibration and gives more weight to the calibration patients who resemble the target hospital's mix of ill and healthy, a mix it has to estimate from the target's scores, since the target's diagnoses are unknown. Appendix H reports it.

Every patient ends in one of three places: the right answer alone, a referral, or the wrong answer alone. An ill patient is recognised, referred or missed; a healthy patient is cleared, referred or falsely flagged. Each share is a share of all the ill, or of all the healthy. A referred patient therefore stays in the count as neither right nor wrong, which lets an option that refers be compared with one that does not. The share of the ill caught is the recognised and the referred together, and nothing below counts a referred patient as recognised.

### 2.4 Evaluation

Every figure was read on patients who played no part in setting the cut-offs, and repeated over many random splits so that no single split carries a result.

For infarction, PTB-XL's test part was split in half at random 200 times, keeping each patient's tracings together. Each time, one half set the cut-offs, and the other half and the two Chinese hospitals received them. Each infarction figure is the average over those 200 splits.

To see what a site could notice without knowing the diagnoses, five recording faults were applied in software to PTB-XL's test part and the tracings scored again, with the cut-offs set on the tracings as recorded: the arm electrodes swapped; every lead's amplitude scaled by 0.8 and by 1.25, as a machine calibrated to the wrong standard would record; a slow 0.3 Hz drift of 0.5 mV added, as breathing and electrode movement would; and every lead's polarity inverted. Appendix I describes how they were scored.

For structural heart disease, each figure comes with a 95% confidence interval; Appendix H gives the methods. To test whether milder disease explains the loss, the ill outpatients were weighted so that, as a group, they had the same mix of severity as the ill inpatients: the same proportions with one finding or with several, and the same spread of ejection fraction (35 or less, 36 to 45, above 45%). The rule was decided before any result by severity was looked at. If the weighted outpatients were caught at 90%, severity would explain the whole loss; if they were caught no more often than before, it would explain none of it.

To measure what local diagnoses repair, the target's patients were split once into two halves. The cut-offs were reset on a growing number of ECGs from the first half, and checked on the second. At Chongqing the second half holds {{ts.n_eval}} tracings, and the cut-offs were reset on up to 2,000 tracings from the first half, used alone or added to PTB-XL's calibration patients. At Columbia the second half holds {{ladder_eval}} outpatients, {{ladder_eval_ill}} of them ill, and the cut-offs were reset on 25 to 400 ECGs picked at random from the first half; each number was tried {{ladder_draws}} times with different picks (draws).

### 2.5 Five corpora in the calibration role

One collection setting cut-offs and two receiving them cannot tell a general effect of moving cut-offs from something particular to PTB-XL and Chongqing. Five collections therefore took turns at setting the cut-offs: PTB-XL, Shandong, Chapman-Shaoxing with Ningbo, Georgia, and CPSC 2018 with its extension, the last three from the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021 [25]. Each was trained and its cut-offs set on its own ECGs, and its cut-offs were then used unchanged at each of the other four collections: twenty moves for each diagnosis.

Infarction is not recorded across those collections, so the five rotate on five diagnoses that are: sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, left bundle-branch block, right bundle-branch block and first-degree atrioventricular block. Each is a yes-or-no question on its own, so the share caught means the same as for infarction. Shandong's "Normal ECG" describes a whole tracing rather than the rhythm, so sinus rhythm is left out at Shandong, which leaves it twelve moves instead of twenty. Appendix D gives how the diagnoses were matched across collections, the sizes used, and how tracings filed twice were found.

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Where the threshold was set

Where the cut-offs were set, the per-diagnosis option caught 90% of the ill, and the pooled option did not: it met its 90% over all patients by answering the healthy majority well. Figure 1 shows how. Three quarters of PTB-XL's calibration patients have no infarction. When the 90% is counted over everyone, the cheapest way to reach it is to answer those patients correctly, so the pooled option places its cut-offs at higher scores than the single cut-off, and more infarctions fall below them. The per-diagnosis option cannot do this, because its cut-off for the ill is placed using the ill alone.

![Figure 1](results/figures/fig1_thresholds.png)

Figure 1. Where each option places its cut-offs on the infarction score, PTB-XL test part. Grey: {{d.fold10_non_mi}} patients without infarction. Coral: {{inf.fold10_mi}} with infarction. Dashed lines mark the cut-offs; the labelled bands show the answer given in each range of scores. In the figure, "class-conditional" is the per-diagnosis option, "deferred" means referred, and "MI" is myocardial infarction.

The pooled option gave no wrong answer to {{s.none.ptbxl.all}} of all patients but caught only {{o.ptbxl.pooled.mi.cov}} of infarctions, calling {{o.ptbxl.pooled.mi.wrong}} of them healthy, against {{o.ptbxl.plain.mi.wrong}} under the single cut-off (Table 1, Figure 2). It met its target, because that target was counted over all patients, not over the ill. The per-diagnosis option caught {{d.perlabel_within_each}} of the ill and gave no wrong answer to the same share of the healthy.

![Figure 2](results/figures/fig2_outcomes.png)

Figure 2. What each option answers to the patients with and without infarction at PTB-XL, averaged over 200 splits. The test part holds {{inf.fold10_mi}} patients with infarction and {{d.fold10_non_mi}} without, and each split reads about half. The single cut-off and the per-diagnosis option miss the same infarctions; the pooled option misses {{h.ptbxl.pooled.mi.wrong}}%.

Table 1. What each option answers at PTB-XL, per 100 patients with infarction and per 100 without.

| Answer | Single cut-off | Pooled | Per-diagnosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Infarction, called healthy (missed) | {{h.ptbxl.plain.mi.wrong}} | {{h.ptbxl.pooled.mi.wrong}} | **{{h.ptbxl.perlabel.mi.wrong}}** |
| Infarction, referred to a doctor | {{h.ptbxl.plain.mi.deferred}} | {{h.ptbxl.pooled.mi.deferred}} | {{h.ptbxl.perlabel.mi.deferred}} |
| No infarction, called ill (false alarm) | {{h.ptbxl.plain.non.wrong}} | **{{h.ptbxl.pooled.non.wrong}}** | {{h.ptbxl.perlabel.non.wrong}} |
| No infarction, referred to a doctor | {{h.ptbxl.plain.non.deferred}} | {{h.ptbxl.pooled.non.deferred}} | {{h.ptbxl.perlabel.non.deferred}} |

Whether the per-diagnosis option looks better or worse depends on what it is compared with. Against the single cut-off, it missed the same infarctions, about {{d.mi_miss_whole}}, and lowered false alarms from {{o.ptbxl.plain.non.wrong}} to {{o.ptbxl.perlabel.non.wrong}} of patients without infarction. It did so by referring those patients, not by getting them right: the share correctly cleared stayed at {{o.ptbxl.plain.non.correct}} under both. Against the pooled option, it raised false alarms from {{o.ptbxl.pooled.non.wrong}} to {{o.ptbxl.perlabel.non.wrong}} and cut missed infarctions from {{o.ptbxl.pooled.mi.wrong}} to {{o.ptbxl.perlabel.mi.wrong}}.

The same gap appears in the five rotation collections, so it is not particular to PTB-XL. Each collection, reading its own ECGs kept aside for testing with cut-offs counted over all patients, gave no wrong answer to {{rot.none.home.all}} of patients on average but caught {{rot.none.home.diagnosis}} of those with the diagnosis. The gap is wider than for infarction because these diagnoses are rarer, present in a median of {{rot.home_median_prevalence}} of tracings, so the healthy make up almost all of the count. The per-diagnosis option closed the gap on all five collections, catching {{rot.mondrian.home.diagnosis}} of those with the diagnosis. Appendix E gives the figures per collection.

At Columbia the per-diagnosis cut-offs, read on test inpatients, the same setting as the patients that set them, caught {{resnet_sens_in}} of the ill for the trained network, and {{sens_in_low}} to {{sens_in_high}} for the three models with the highest AUROC. Where the cut-offs were set, the per-diagnosis option delivered what it was asked for, in both studies.

### 3.2 Carried to other hospitals

Moved unchanged, the infarction cut-offs caught fewer infarctions at Chongqing and more at Shandong, and across the five collections how much a moved cut-off lost depended mostly on which collection had set it.

At Shandong, the pooled option caught {{s.none.sph.mi}} of infarctions, above the 90% asked for. With the cut-off fixed, whether an ill patient is caught depends only on that patient's score, and Shandong's infarctions score higher than PTB-XL's. The healthy did well there too: {{s.none.sph.non}} were not falsely flagged. The per-diagnosis option, whose cut-off for the ill sits lower than the pooled one, caught {{s.mondrian.sph.mi}}. At Chongqing, the pooled option caught {{s.none.acs.mi}} of infarctions, {{d.acs_shortfall}} points short of the 90%, and the per-diagnosis option {{s.mondrian.acs.mi}}, still short. Patients without infarction lost more than those with it: the share not falsely flagged fell from {{s.none.ptbxl.non}} at PTB-XL to {{s.none.acs.non}} under the pooled option and {{s.mondrian.acs.non}} under the per-diagnosis option. Whatever changed at Chongqing affected the healthy as well as the ill.

![Figure 3](results/figures/fig3_coverage.png)

Figure 3. Share of patients given no wrong answer at each hospital (rows: PTB-XL {{inf.ptbxl_n}} tracings, Shandong {{inf.sph_n}}, Chongqing {{inf.acs_n}}) under each option (columns: pooled; "class-conditional", the per-diagnosis option; "label-shift weighted", the fourth option). Within each panel, the share asked for rises from left to right. Grey: all patients. Blue: patients without infarction. Red: patients with infarction. Dashed line: the share asked for. Each bar is an average over 200 splits of PTB-XL; its thin line shows how much the result varies between splits.

In the terms a clinician uses, the single cut-off set for 90% sensitivity caught {{o.acs.plain.mi.correct}} of infarctions at Chongqing and {{o.sph.plain.mi.correct}} at Shandong. The per-diagnosis option catches the same infarctions; of its {{s.mondrian.acs.mi}} at Chongqing, {{o.acs.perlabel.mi.correct}} were called ill and {{o.acs.perlabel.mi.deferred}} referred. The single cut-off's specificity fell from {{o.ptbxl.plain.non.correct}} at PTB-XL to {{o.acs.plain.non.correct}} at Chongqing. On patients without infarction at Chongqing, the per-diagnosis option did worse than the pooled one: it flagged {{o.acs.perlabel.non.wrong}} of them as infarction and referred {{o.acs.perlabel.non.deferred}}, where the pooled option flagged {{o.acs.pooled.non.wrong}} and referred {{o.acs.pooled.non.deferred}}. The fourth option misjudged the share of infarction at both hospitals and caught no more than the per-diagnosis option (Appendix H).

Across the five collections, moved cut-offs lost or gained, and which collection set them mattered more than the average. Once moved, the per-diagnosis option caught {{rot.mondrian.away.diagnosis}} of the ill on average, against 90% asked, and the worst single move, CPSC's sinus-rhythm cut-off used on PTB-XL, {{rot.bias.worst_pair}}. So the gain at Shandong and the loss at Chongqing were not chance: moving a cut-off can push the share caught either way, by a large amount, depending on where it was set. In a few moves the cut-off for the ill could not be placed at all, because the collection that set it had too few ill patients with that diagnosis; Figure 4 rings them, and Appendix E gives their figures.

![Figure 4](results/figures/fig7_rotation.png)

Figure 4. Share of the ill caught for each diagnosis, asked for 90%, under each option, every move drawn. Columns are the five diagnoses, panels the three options ("class-conditional" is the per-diagnosis option, "label-shift weighted" the fourth). Filled dots are moved cut-offs, coloured by the collection that set them; the hollow marker is that collection reading its own ECGs kept aside for testing. Bars are the average over moves, with the spread across collections. A ringed marker is a move whose cut-off for the ill could not be placed, so the result does not measure the option answering (Appendix E).

### 3.3 Carried to the outpatients of the same hospital

Moved from Columbia's inpatients to its outpatients, cut-offs asked to catch 90% of the ill caught about {{strongest_about}}, for every one of the three models with the highest AUROC.

The per-diagnosis cut-offs set on inpatients caught {{e.resnet.outpatient.perlabel.pos}} of the outpatients who have moderate or worse structural heart disease on echocardiography, did not falsely flag {{e.resnet.outpatient.perlabel.neg}} of those who do not, and referred {{e.resnet.outpatient.perlabel.abst}} of outpatients to a doctor. In the emergency department they caught {{emergency_sens}} of the ill, and among test inpatients {{resnet_sens_in}}. Outpatients with an ejection fraction of 45% or less were caught more often: {{lvef_sens_out}}. The pooled option caught {{pool.resnet_pooled_out}} of the ill outpatients for the composite. For {{w.pool.zero_findings}} rarer findings (aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, pericardial effusion), taken one at a time, it caught no ill outpatient at all: with so few ill patients, cut-offs counted over everyone are placed for the healthy.

The loss is not one model's. The three models with the highest AUROC lost the same: {{e.resnet.outpatient.perlabel.pos}} of the ill outpatients caught for the trained ResNet and for ECGFounder, {{e.echonext_mini.outpatient.perlabel.pos}} for the published mini-model (Table 2). A network trained here, one trained by the EchoNext authors and one trained elsewhere all fall to the same level, which points at the outpatients' ECGs rather than at one model. All three learned from the same EchoNext training patients, though, so their agreement is weaker evidence than three separate studies would give. The untrained model loses less only because it refers more outpatients, and a referred patient counts as caught.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

"Frozen, probes": used as released, with a small final step fitted on EchoNext. "Random initialisation": the untrained network of section 2.2.

In patient terms, the per-diagnosis option misses the same ill outpatients as the single cut-off. Of the ill outpatients, it calls {{recognised_low}} to {{recognised_high}} ill, for the three models, and refers a further {{referred_low}} to {{referred_high}} to a doctor (Table 3). It clears the same healthy outpatients as the single cut-off and refers most of the others instead of flagging them, so its false alarms fall to {{false_alarm_low}} to {{false_alarm_high}} of the healthy outpatients, at the price of referring {{referred_all_low}} to {{referred_all_high}} of all outpatients.

| Model | Ill, recognised | Ill, referred | Ill, missed | Healthy, cleared | Healthy, referred | Healthy, falsely flagged | All referred |

### 3.4 What a site sees without knowing the diagnoses

A site running a model without fresh diagnoses can watch two figures: the AUROC it was shown when it adopted the model, and the share of patients referred. Neither showed the loss.

At Columbia, the AUROC did not show it. Among test inpatients the trained network's AUROC was {{resnet_auroc_in}}, and among outpatients {{resnet_auroc_out}}, with overlapping confidence intervals for every model, while the share of the ill it caught fell from {{resnet_sens_in}} to {{resnet_sens_out}} (Figure 5). Moving a cut-off up or down trades sensitivity against specificity, and the AUROC sums up that whole trade-off, not the point where the cut-off sits. Among outpatients the trade-off was almost the same, but the same cut-off sat at a point of lower sensitivity and higher specificity: for the three models, the single cut-off's specificity rose from {{spec_in_low}}–{{spec_in_high}} among test inpatients to {{spec_out_low}}–{{spec_out_high}} among outpatients. A report of AUROC by care setting therefore reads as a success.

![Figure 5](results/figures/fig9_care_settings.png)

Figure 5. AUROC (left) and the sensitivity of the cut-off set on inpatients (right) in each care setting of the EchoNext test part, for the four models. Dashed line: the 90% the cut-off was set for.

Between hospitals, the AUROC moved in the same direction as the share caught but did not measure it. The infarction network's AUROC was {{inf.baseline_auroc}} at PTB-XL, {{sph_auroc}} at Shandong, where more infarctions were caught, and {{acs_auroc}} at Chongqing, where fewer were. It gave no hint of the size of the change at Chongqing: the single cut-off's sensitivity fell from 90% to {{o.acs.plain.mi.correct}}, and its specificity from {{o.ptbxl.plain.non.correct}} to {{o.acs.plain.non.correct}}.

A recording fault can even move every score without moving the AUROC. The AUROC depends only on which patients score higher than which. Scaling every lead by 0.8 raised the scores nearly together, so their order, and the AUROC, barely changed ({{p.gain_080.auroc}} against {{p.clean.auroc}}), but the fixed cut-off now sat lower among them, and the share of patients without infarction not falsely flagged fell {{d.gain_non_mi_fall}} points.

Table 4. The per-diagnosis option under recording faults, PTB-XL test part. Shares are averages over the same 200 splits.

| Condition | AUROC | Infarctions caught | No infarction, not falsely flagged | All patients, no wrong answer | Referred |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| As recorded | {{p.clean.auroc}} | {{p.clean.mi}} | {{p.clean.non}} | {{p.clean.all}} | {{p.clean.deferred}} |
| Arm electrodes exchanged | {{p.limb_reversal.auroc}} | {{p.limb_reversal.mi}} | {{p.limb_reversal.non}} | {{p.limb_reversal.all}} | {{p.limb_reversal.deferred}} |
| Every lead × 0.8 | {{p.gain_080.auroc}} | {{p.gain_080.mi}} | {{p.gain_080.non}} | {{p.gain_080.all}} | {{p.gain_080.deferred}} |
| Every lead × 1.25 | {{p.gain_125.auroc}} | {{p.gain_125.mi}} | {{p.gain_125.non}} | {{p.gain_125.all}} | {{p.gain_125.deferred}} |
| Baseline wander added | {{p.baseline_wander.auroc}} | {{p.baseline_wander.mi}} | {{p.baseline_wander.non}} | {{p.baseline_wander.all}} | {{p.baseline_wander.deferred}} |
| Polarity inverted | {{p.polarity.auroc}} | {{p.polarity.mi}} | {{p.polarity.non}} | {{p.polarity.all}} | {{p.polarity.deferred}} |

The share referred did not follow the damage either. Swapping the arm electrodes took the share of all patients given no wrong answer from {{p.clean.all}}% to {{p.limb_reversal.all}}%, and the share referred moved by only {{d.limb_deferral_move}} points, from {{p.clean.deferred}}% to {{p.limb_reversal.deferred}}%. Inverting the polarity made the model worse than a coin toss (AUROC {{p.polarity.auroc}}) and took the share given no wrong answer to {{p.polarity.all}}%, yet the share referred *fell*, to {{p.polarity.deferred}}%. Baseline wander was the one fault the referrals showed, because it pushed many scores into the grey zone (Appendix I). A rising share of infarctions caught is no reassurance either. Swapping the electrodes and inverting the polarity raised most scores, so nearly every patient was flagged: infarctions caught rose to {{p.limb_reversal.mi}}% and {{p.polarity.mi}}%, while most patients without infarction were flagged too. At Columbia, with no fault, the share referred moved in the reassuring direction: for the trained network it fell from {{resnet_referred_in}} among test inpatients to {{resnet_referred_out}} among outpatients, while the share of the ill caught fell from {{resnet_sens_in}} to {{resnet_sens_out}}.

### 3.5 Why the coverage fell

The ill patients scored differently at the target, and the two moves point at different reasons: at Chongqing what counts as an infarction changed along with everything else, while at Columbia part of the loss is milder disease.

The per-diagnosis cut-off for the ill is placed using the ill alone, so a change in how common the disease is cannot by itself lower the share caught; where that share still fell, the ill patients themselves scored lower. At Chongqing, an infarction is a discharge diagnosis of acute infarction rather than an ECG finding, and the scores of both ill and healthy patients differ from PTB-XL's, those of the healthy more. The definition, the population, the recording machines and the years all differ between PTB-XL and Chongqing, and this design measures their combined effect without separating them.

At Columbia the definition is the same. Severity explains about a third of the lost coverage. The ill outpatients are ill more mildly than the ill inpatients who set the cut-offs: they carry fewer of the eleven findings, keep a higher ejection fraction, and have less right ventricular dysfunction, tricuspid regurgitation and pericardial effusion, with aortic stenosis the exception (Table F1). With the inpatient cut-offs, outpatients with two findings or more are caught more often than those with one, and those with an ejection fraction of 45% or less more often than those above it (Table 5).

Table 5. Ill outpatients caught, by severity, and after weighting them to the inpatients' mix of severity; 95% confidence intervals in brackets.

| Model | Ill outpatients caught | One finding, {{sev.n_one}} | Two or more, {{sev.n_two}} | Ejection fraction 35 or less, {{sev.n_le35}} | 36 to 45, {{sev.n_36}} | Above 45, {{sev.n_gt45}} | Weighted to the inpatients' severity | Share of the loss explained |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{rows:severity_rows_named}}

Weighted to the inpatients' severity, the ill outpatients would be caught at {{sev.reweighted_range}}, still short of 90%. Severity therefore closes {{sev.share_range}} of the gap between what was caught and 90%, for the three models. The rest of the loss sits within each level of severity. Of the {{sev.above_45_n}} ill outpatients whose ejection fraction is above 45%, {{sev.above_45_range}} are caught; the inpatients who set the cut-offs, in the same band, are caught at {{sev.above_45_inpatient_range}}, a figure read on the very ECGs that set the cut-off and so likely higher than on new patients. The weighting uses six groups, each combining the number of findings with an ejection fraction band; {{low:sev.cells_unjudged}} them hold fewer than 30 ill outpatients and are not judged one by one.

In neither move did a different model repair the loss. At Columbia three models built in different ways fell alike, and for infarction five other networks, each trained beforehand on other ECGs, did no better at Chongqing (Appendix E).

### 3.6 What repaired it: the receiving site's own labels

In both moves, a hundred ECGs with known diagnoses from the target did what no option and no model did: reset on them, the cut-offs caught close to 90% of the ill again.

At Chongqing, PTB-XL's pooled cut-offs caught {{ts.none.recalibrated.0}} of infarctions among the {{ts.n_eval}} tracings kept aside for checking. Reset on 100 Chongqing tracings, they caught {{ts.none.recalibrated.100}}; on 500 and 2,000, {{ts.none.recalibrated.500}} and {{ts.none.recalibrated.2000}} (Figure 6). Adding the same Chongqing tracings to PTB-XL's calibration patients, instead of using them alone, helped far less: {{ts.none.pooled.100}} with 100, {{ts.none.pooled.2000}} with 2,000. What repairs the cut-off is being set on the target's own patients, not the number of patients it is set on. Under the per-diagnosis option, the same reset raised the infarctions caught from {{ts.mondrian.recalibrated.0}} to {{ts.mondrian.recalibrated.100}}, and a hundred Chongqing tracings hold about {{inf.ladder_100_mi}} infarctions.

![Figure 6](results/figures/fig8_target_scale.png)

Figure 6. Share of infarctions caught at Chongqing against the number of Chongqing tracings with known diagnoses the cut-off was reset on, starting from PTB-XL's cut-off, 90% asked for. Zero is PTB-XL's cut-off unchanged, the same point on both lines. "Recalibrated" uses the Chongqing tracings alone; "pooled" adds them to PTB-XL's calibration patients.

At Columbia, on the half of the outpatients kept for checking, the inpatient cut-offs caught {{el.resnet.0.cov}} of the ill; reset on 100 outpatient ECGs from the other half, {{el.resnet.100.cov}}, and {{el.resnet.100.neg}} of the healthy were not falsely flagged (Table 6). Most of the gain came from patients called ill: with the inpatient cut-offs, the trained network called {{el.resnet.0.recognised}} of the ill outpatients ill and referred {{el.resnet.0.referred}}; after the reset, it called {{el.resnet.100.recognised}} ill and referred {{el.resnet.100.referred}}. A hundred outpatient ECGs hold about {{el.fit_ill_mean}} ill patients, between {{el.fit_ill_min}} and {{el.fit_ill_max}} in a given draw, so the cut-off for the ill rests on a couple of dozen patients. Fewer than 100 did not work. At 25 ECGs, which hold about {{el.fit_ill_25_mean}} ill patients and in some draws only {{el.fit_ill_25_min}}, there were too few ill patients to place the cut-off for the ill in {{ladder_25_flagged}} of draws, and every patient was then flagged or referred.

## 4. Discussion

A cut-off set to catch 90% of the ill at one place caught a different share at another, in both moves, because the ill patients scored differently there. A hundred local ECGs with known diagnoses brought it back, and nothing a site sees without diagnoses warned of the loss.

Across hospitals the infarction cut-off missed its target at both sites, below it at Chongqing and above it at Shandong, and five collections taking turns showed that the direction and size of the change depend on which collection set the cut-off. Inside one hospital, where the definition of the disease stayed the same, the per-diagnosis cut-off that caught {{resnet_sens_in}} of ill inpatients caught {{resnet_sens_out}} of ill outpatients, and three models built in different ways lost the same. The target's own ECGs repaired the loss in both: a hundred brought the share of the ill caught to within about a point of 90%, or above it, on average, though one draw in ten still fell below 90% on EchoNext.

The figure a target site is shown does not answer that question. The EchoNext authors read a stable AUROC across care settings as a sign that the model is stable [17,18]; on the same data the AUROC held while the share of the ill caught fell, because the cut-off moved along an almost unchanged trade-off between sensitivity and specificity. Published ECG studies show the same: an AUROC of 0.82 kept in a Russian population came with a sensitivity of 26.9% [19]. Only the cut-off's own figures showed the loss. The EchoNext authors' community study attributes its fall in AUROC to milder disease [22], which this study found explains about a third of the loss at Columbia.

Where the cut-offs were set, a 90% counted over all patients was compatible with failing many of the ill: {{s.none.ptbxl.all}} of all patients against {{s.none.ptbxl.mi}} of infarctions, in a cohort where {{d.ptbxl_prevalence_whole}} have one. Others have reported the same on skin lesions, in drug screening and on the ECG [5,6,12,15]. The gap is larger here than El Allam and Hamlich found on the ECG, because PTB-XL is used here to tell infarction from every other ECG, not only from normal ones, and infarction is rarer in that comparison ({{d.ptbxl_prevalence_whole}} against 36.4%), so a count over all patients leans more on those without it. A single figure over all patients says close to nothing about the ill when they are few, and any such tool should report the share caught for each diagnosis.

Most of the benefit does not need conformal prediction. A rule described by Chow in 1970 refers the patients between two plain cut-offs, each placed at the score that 90% of one diagnosis's calibration patients pass [16]. It gives the same results as the per-diagnosis option at all three infarction sites, within half a percentage point, while referring slightly fewer patients. What does the work is setting a cut-off for each diagnosis separately. Conformal prediction adds a small adjustment that makes the 90% hold exactly even when the calibration group is small, worth less than half a point at PTB-XL, and a name and a target for what a site should measure. Appendix E gives the figures, and the same comparison across the five collections, where the adjustment counts for more because the ill calibration patients are fewer.

Against current practice, the per-diagnosis option offers fewer false alarms for the same number of missed patients, and the false alarms it removes become referrals, not correct answers. At PTB-XL a doctor reads roughly one ECG in ten in exchange for {{w.false_alarms_saved}} points fewer false alarms; at Columbia {{referred_all_low}} to {{referred_all_high}} of outpatients are referred to bring false alarms down to {{false_alarm_low}} to {{false_alarm_high}}. Whether that trade is worth it turns on the cost of a missed diagnosis, an unnecessary workup and a doctor's time, none of which this study evaluates. A reader study in which 62 cardiologists read 20 ECG cases tested whether clinicians decide better when shown a set of possible answers than when shown one. They were more accurate with sets, by a moderate amount (an effect size of 0.53 on complex cases and 0.67 among cardiologists with under ten years' experience, where 0.5 is conventionally moderate), and more so with a written explanation (0.62). The study was designed to show that sets were no worse than single answers, with a margin of -0.20, so it says a referral route is acceptable to readers, not what it costs [8].

The two moves lost for different reasons. At Chongqing the definition of an infarction moved with the patients, and this design cannot separate the two; at Shandong, where mainly the share of infarction changed, nothing failed. A loss after a move between hospitals is therefore shown at Chongqing alone, the one site whose change the design cannot take apart. The move from inpatients to outpatients supplies what that design lacks: the definition stayed the same and the share caught still fell. Milder disease accounts for about a third of the fall, and the rest remains within each level of severity: of the ill outpatients whose ejection fraction is above 45%, {{sev.above_45_range}} are caught, against {{sev.above_45_inpatient_range}} of the inpatients who set the cut-offs, in the same band. What else sets them apart, the type of finding, age, a coexisting rhythm, or something in the ECG the diagnosis does not record, is not measured here. Six groups are a coarse measure of severity, so they probably leave some of its effect unmeasured [belief: coarse groups leave severity differences inside each one].

What a site adopting such a model should do follows from both moves. It should count, on its own patients, the share of the ill each cut-off catches, for each diagnosis, since neither the figure over all patients nor the AUROC carries it. That count needs ill patients more than ECGs: to know the share caught to within two percentage points either way, with 95% confidence, takes {{aux.mi_cases_needed}} infarctions, which is {{aux.tracings.acs}} tracings at Chongqing's share of infarction and {{aux.tracings.sph}} at Shandong's. To reset the cut-off rather than to check it, about a hundred ECGs with known diagnoses from the target moved the cut-off most of the way in both moves, at the price of more false alarms: the share of the healthy not falsely flagged fell from {{healthy_before}} to {{healthy_after}} for the trained network at Columbia. Twenty-five ECGs were not enough, and a hundred outpatients hold only a couple of dozen ill. Neither the share referred nor the AUROC replaces known diagnoses: at Columbia both stayed quiet while the share caught fell. And a site should expect its own result to differ from any one published move: across the five collections, the share caught after a move varied by up to {{rot.sd_points}} percentage points (one standard deviation) depending on which collection set the cut-off.

## 5. Limitations

The study counts missed and referred patients, not what happens to them, and it rests on few moves. Each point below says what a reader should not conclude.

No clinical outcome was measured. A referral is a workload, not a benefit: whether sending one ECG in ten to a doctor improves care depends on who reads it and how fast, neither of which was measured. At Columbia the per-diagnosis option refers {{resnet_referred_out}} of outpatients and {{resnet_referred_in}} of test inpatients for the trained network, and whether a clinic can absorb that was not measured either.

The moves are few. For infarction there are two target hospitals, one diagnosis and one source, and the two targets moved in opposite directions, so neither the direction nor the size of the effect can be assumed at a third site. The five collections widen that to twenty moves per diagnosis, on other diagnoses. The EchoNext move stays inside one hospital, whose ECGs all come from one manufacturer's machines.

Between hospitals, causes are mixed. Recording machines, population, years and the definition of the disease all differ between PTB-XL and the target hospitals, so the design measures the resulting change without attributing it to any one of them.

The guarantee is about groups, not about one patient. The share caught is an average over the patients with a diagnosis. The per-diagnosis guarantee is stated for the ill and for the healthy separately, and when an ECG is read nobody yet knows which group the patient is in, so it cannot be turned into a statement about that patient.

The variation quoted with the infarction figures understates the uncertainty. It shows how much a result changes from one split of PTB-XL to another, with the target hospitals held fixed, which is smaller than a confidence interval. At Shandong it is {{s.none.sph.sd_mi_points}} points, while a 95% confidence interval on Shandong's own {{inf.sph_mi_n}} infarctions runs from {{inf.sph_pooled_wilson}}. The 90% asked for sits inside that interval, so the {{s.none.sph.mi}} caught there is not evidence of catching more than asked. The differences the study rests on survive the wider intervals (Appendix H).

No difference by sex or age is established for the per-diagnosis option. Appendix G gives the share caught by sex and age at PTB-XL. The only difference there clearly beyond chance is that patients without infarction aged 75 and over were falsely flagged more often than younger ones. Within infarction the groups are small, {{sg.women_mi_n}} women and {{sg.old_mi_n}} patients aged 75 and over, too few to settle a difference. Sex and age are the two groups PTB-XL records; the target hospitals publish nothing that would allow the same breakdown. At Columbia the share of ill outpatients caught is {{women}} for women and {{men}} for men, a single look not adjusted for the number of comparisons made, which could be chance.

One target, 90%, and one way of turning the model's score into the conformal answer were used throughout. Appendix H gives what changes with another. The choice of 90% is conventional and not weighed against any particular clinical cost.

The share caught is not the positive predictive value, the chance that a flagged patient has the disease, which depends directly on how common the disease is. For infarction under the per-diagnosis option it is {{inf.sph_ppv}} at Shandong, {{inf.acs_ppv}} at Chongqing and {{inf.ptbxl_ppv}} at PTB-XL.

The faults were applied in software, at PTB-XL only, one at a time and at one strength each. A real site's faults reach some tracings, in combination, at strengths nobody chose. They show that the share referred can stay flat while the share caught collapses, not how often that happens.

In a few moves among the five collections, the cut-off for the ill could not be placed because the collection setting it had too few ill patients with that diagnosis; every patient is then flagged or referred, which looks like a high share caught. Appendix E counts those moves and gives the averages with and without them. At Columbia, resetting the cut-offs on fewer than 100 ECGs meets the same limit.

Each of the five collections' networks, and the EchoNext ResNet, was trained once, from one random starting point, so the spread between collections and between EchoNext models also carries the chance variation of a single training run.

Three of the five networks compared for infarction in Appendix E had seen collections used here during their earlier training, and their published descriptions are the only record of that, so they cannot be ranked against each other and no result rests on them.

Severity is only partly measured. Six groups of findings and ejection fraction explain {{share_low}} to {{share_high}} of the EchoNext loss. They do not describe all that distinguishes an ill outpatient, and the comparison within each band is against the ECGs that set the cut-off.

The earlier SSRN preprint (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5944060, deposited 26 December 2025) carries different figures under a different title; neither the 10.44% nor the 51.9% it reports appears anywhere in the published paper, and this report cites the published version only.

## Declarations

**Competing interests.** The author has worked at Idoven, which develops ECG analysis software. Idoven had no part in the design, conduct, funding or reporting of this study, took no view on its results, and none of its data, models or software were used.

**Funding.** None.

**Data.** All three infarction datasets are public. PTB-XL and the four auxiliary PhysioNet corpora were downloaded on 23 August 2026; the Shandong dataset and the Chongqing dataset from figshare on the same date. Access dates and checksums are recorded in `scripts/fetch_open_corpora.sh` and `results/ingest_report.json`. EchoNext is under PhysioNet's restricted licence. Its tracings, and the per-record scores computed from them, stay outside this repository; the results hold counts and aggregate figures only.

**Ethics.** This is a secondary analysis of seven publicly released, de-identified ECG datasets and one released under PhysioNet's credentialed access. Patients were not contacted, and no further approval was sought. The approvals under which each dataset was released are as follows. PTB-XL: the Institutional Ethics Committee approved publication of the anonymous data in an open-access database, reference PTB-2020-1; the source publication states no participant consent procedure. SPH: approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shandong Provincial Hospital, with the requirement for individual patient consent waived and public sharing permitted after de-identification; no approval number is given. ACS-ECG: approved by the ethics committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, approval number 2024-256-01, with written informed consent waived as the study is retrospective and all patient identifiers removed. EchoNext: released under the approval of the Columbia University institutional review board, with patient consent waived [18]. The release approvals of the four Challenge-2021 corpora (Chapman-Shaoxing, Ningbo, Georgia and CPSC) were not checked for this report. No attempt was made to re-identify any patient, and nothing this repository publishes would permit it.

**Not a device.** This is a retrospective measurement study on public data. It makes no claim as a device or about patient outcomes, and it has no regulatory status.

## Data and code

Tables 1 and 4 come from `results/outcomes.json` and `results/perturbations.json`; Tables 2 and 6 and Figure 5 from `results/echonext_transfer.json`; Table 3 from `results/echonext_outcomes.json`; Table 5 from `results/echonext_severity.json`. Numbers: `results/outcomes.json` (per-label outcomes and decision boundaries), `results/shift.json` (coverage per site and correction), `results/subgroups.json` (coverage within sex and age), `results/auxiliary.json` (the quantities the discussion and limitations argue from, and the AUROC at each infarction site), `results/perturbations.json` with the score arrays in `results/perturbations.npz`, `results/abstention.json`, `results/baseline.json`. `results/arms.json` holds the comparison of five encoders; it records the seed it was drawn with, and Appendix E quotes it for the two AUROCs at the ends of its range, for the coverage each arm reaches at the three sites, and for which corpora each arm was pretrained on. The rotation adds `results/label_map.json`, `results/duplicate_groups.json` and `results/split_leak.json`, `results/rotation.csv` with `results/rotation.json`, `results/rotation_uncertainty.csv` with its own summary, and `results/target_scale.json`. EchoNext adds `results/echonext_transfer.json` with `results/echonext_coverage.csv` (cohorts, AUROC, the coverage grid, the ladder with its split and its count of the ill per draw, subgroups), `results/echonext_outcomes.json` (the recognised, referred and missed), `results/echonext_severity.json` and `results/echonext_provenance.json`, written by the scripts of the same names. The two infarction files `outcomes.json` and `shift.json` are built by separate scripts that draw the same 200 patient-level splits, so the same quantity agrees between them; the source-site decomposition is quoted from `outcomes.json` throughout and the per-site coverage from `shift.json`. `scripts/outcomes.py` builds the outcome table, `scripts/subgroups.py` the subgroup table, and `scripts/figures.py` redraws every figure, pixel for pixel, from a committed results file. That script numbers its files in its own order, so figure 4 here is `fig7_rotation.png`, figure 5 is `fig9_care_settings.png` and figure 6 is `fig8_target_scale.png`. Each results file that can be rebuilt from committed inputs carries the digest of every source file its numbers depend on, and a test fails if any of those files has changed since: `results/outcomes.json`, `results/shift.json`, `results/abstention.json`, `results/subgroups.json` and `results/perturbations.json` are therefore the output of the code in this commit. The files that cannot be rebuilt in minutes (the training runs, the two external re-scores, the ingest report, the encoder arms, the EchoNext scores and the two timing files) are named in `tests/test_provenance.py` with the reason. Every number this report prints is a named figure read from one of those files: the text is rendered from `docs/templates/REPORT.md` by `uv run python tests/report_render.py --write`, and `tests/test_report_numbers.py` fails when the committed text differs from that rendering or when the template types a number that is neither a cited figure nor a named constant of the design. Reproduction: `uv sync`, `uv run pytest`, `uv run python scripts/figures.py`, then `uv run python scripts/outcomes.py` and `uv run python scripts/subgroups.py`, which need PTB-XL's `ptbxl_database.csv` for the patient, sex and age of each record; the README gives the timings and the environment variable that points at it.

## Appendix B. The infarction network

Table B1. The network that supplies the frozen infarction scores.

| | |
|---|---|
| Architecture | one-dimensional ResNet after Wang et al. 2017, the shape the PTB-XL benchmark uses: a stem of one 15-wide convolution to 64 channels at stride 2 with batch normalisation and max pooling, then four stages of two residual blocks at widths 64, 128, 256 and 256 with 7-wide kernels, each stage after the first halving the time axis, then global average pooling and a linear head to two classes. 4,082,306 parameters |
| Input | 12 leads in the order I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF, V1 to V6, 500 Hz, ten seconds, 5,000 samples, in millivolts. One centre and one spread over all leads, taken from the training fold alone and applied unchanged everywhere: {{base.centre}} mV and {{base.scale}} mV |
| Objective | cross-entropy with equal class weights, on the training fold as recorded, without resampling or augmentation |
| Optimiser | AdamW, learning rate 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻², batch size 64 |
| Stopping | at most {{base.epochs}} epochs, stopping after {{base.patience}} without a better validation AUROC on fold 9. Epoch {{base.epoch_kept}} was the best and was kept, so the run stopped at epoch {{d.epoch_stopped}} |
| Seed | 0, for the weights and for the batch order |
| Hardware and time | six-core Intel i7-8700, CPU only, six threads, PyTorch 2.2.2 on Python 3.11.15; {{base.seconds}} seconds, {{w.base_duration}} |
| Determinism | the seed fixes a run at a given thread count. Two runs of the training step agree bit for bit at one thread and at four; a one-thread run and a four-thread run of the same seed differ in every one of the 62 parameter tensors after six batches, by up to 4·10⁻³. Reproducing the checkpoint needs the six threads the hardware row records, and reproducing the AUROC to its third decimal does not |
| What it reports | one probability per class for infarction. AUROC {{inf.baseline_auroc}}, 95% interval {{inf.baseline_low}} to {{inf.baseline_high}}; area under the precision-recall curve {{base.auprc}}, {{base.auprc_low}} to {{base.auprc_high}}; on fold 10, {{inf.fold10}} tracings, {{inf.fold10_mi}} of them infarction |
| What it is for | supplying frozen scores so that three threshold placements can be compared on identical inputs |
| What it is not for | any clinical use, any diagnosis other than infarction, and any site: it was fitted on one German research corpus recorded between 1989 and 1996 |

Every value above is recorded in `results/baseline/config.json` and `results/baseline/metrics.json`, or is the setting `scripts/train_baseline.py` applies, with two exceptions: the parameter count is a property of the architecture, recorded in `results/timing.json`, and the determinism row reports a probe of the training step. The nearest published anchor for this architecture and split is {{base.anchor}}, a macro average over the five PTB-XL superclasses rather than the infarction column, so the agreement is a plausibility check and not a reproduction. The benchmark does not report the infarction column separately, and its archived predictions link to another study's files; `results/baseline.json` records the anchor and the three routes tried to obtain an infarction-only figure.

## Appendix C. Running the EchoNext arms

The mini-model's weights come from the authors' IntroECG repository (commit 15233e93) and hold tensors only, so `torch.load` reads them with `weights_only=True`. Its architecture is `EchoNextMini` in `src/ecs/echonext_mini.py`, written from the shapes of the checkpoint rather than copied, since the repository states no licence; every tensor of the checkpoint loads into it, with none missing. It reads the tracing as distributed and the seven tabular features the distribution ships already standardised (sex, age, rates and intervals), which the other three arms do not see. Scoring the validation and test splits took {{e.run.mini_seconds}} seconds on the Apple GPU.

ECGFounder's checkpoint holds one numpy scalar beside its tensors, which `weights_only=True` refuses on torch 2.2.2. It is read through an unpickler that resolves five names (the tensor rebuild, an ordered dict, the numpy scalar, its dtype and a byte codec) and refuses any other, so the file is never unpickled in full. Its network is the authors' Net1D, vendored in `third_party/ecgfounder`. The model card asks for 500 Hz, so each tracing is resampled from 250 Hz by polyphase filtering; the amplitude stays in z-score, since no millivolt scale exists to restore. The {{e.run.founder_features}} features before the dense head feed one logistic probe per label. Embedding the {{e.run.store_size}} training, validation and test ECGs and fitting the probes took {{e.run.founder_seconds}} seconds.

EchoNext's tracings have no physical unit. Each lead was median-filtered, clipped at its 0.1st and 99.9th percentiles and standardised with a mean and a standard deviation computed over the training set, so every tracing here is in z-score at 250 Hz, as `results/echonext_provenance.json` records for all {{records}} of them. The authors' code package publishes those per-lead means and standard deviations in the integer counts of the GE MUSE export, without stating how many microvolts a count is, so the millivolt scale cannot be recovered. Moving a model trained here to another hospital means replaying the same preprocessing on that hospital's ECGs, with that hospital's own standardisation, which absorbs part of any difference between electrocardiographs.

## Appendix D. The rotation's labels and splits

The corpora annotate in three schemes, and `results/label_map.json` records the mapping onto the five classes with its counts. Those counts reproduce the Challenge's own published per-partition figures exactly: published minus measured minus the records carrying both halves of a fused pair is zero for every class on {{rot.label_map.challenge_corpora}}. {{cap:rot.label_map.ambiguities}} and each is recorded, among them Shandong's "Normal ECG", a statement about a whole tracing where the Challenge's "sinus rhythm" is a statement about the rhythm, which is why that class is refused on Shandong.

Three of the five corpora file the same tracing under more than one record identifier, and the Challenge collection ships no patient key, so a split by patient treated each copy as a separate patient. Screening the first ten seconds of the twelve canonical leads, quantised to ten microvolts, found {{rot.split.leak_before}} of identical tracings sitting in two parts a figure is read across, {{rot.split.leak_in_cpsc}}, {{rot.split.leak_in_georgia}} and {{rot.split.leak_in_chapman}} with Ningbo, some straddling the boundary between training and test. The splitting unit is therefore the transitive closure over same patient and same recording, and `results/split_leak.json` reports the count before and after, which is zero. {{rot.split.sph_repeats}} and files them under one patient, so its split already held them; PTB-XL's distribution repeats none. On the {{rot.split.digests_compared}} this screen and the one published by the delivery corpus both cover, the two digests agree on every record. {{rot.split.across_corpora}}, so no source-target pair shares a recording.

Training and calibration parts are capped at the size the smallest collection reaches, {{rot.sizes.caps}}, so that no collection is favoured by its size, and a collection is scored on the same test part whether it sets the cut-offs or receives them. The share caught is reported per diagnosis under the three options, as an average over {{rot.sizes.draws}}. Each receiving cohort is also resampled by patient, {{rot.sizes.bootstrap}}, for a percentile interval; both are in `results/rotation_uncertainty.csv`, which repeats every row by sex and by four age bands and flags a cell resting on {{rot.sizes.thin}} of the diagnosis. The same file reports what a rule with one plain empirical quantile per diagnosis reaches on the same scores, which is the per-diagnosis construction minus the finite-sample correction.

## Appendix E. The rotation in detail: per diagnosis, starved thresholds, draw spread and the plain reject rule

In this appendix a pair is one collection's cut-off for one diagnosis (the source) read at another collection (the target), "away" is such a move, and "home" a collection reading its own held-out tracings. The bias of a pair is the share of the diagnosis it catches minus the 90% asked, as a fraction.

At home, reading their own held-out records under pooled calibration, the five corpora {{rot.coverage.none_home_coverage_mean}} {{rot.coverage.none_home_coverage_diagnosis_mean}} the diagnosis they are asked about, averaged over the {{rot.cells.home_cells}}: the target is met over the population and missed by {{w.rot.home_gap}} points inside the label. In {{rot.rarer_n}} of the {{rot.cells.home_n}} home cells the diagnosis is rarer than infarction was, at a median prevalence of {{rot.home_median_prevalence}}; the exception is sinus rhythm on PTB-XL, at {{rot.nsr_ptbxl.prevalence}} prevalence, covered at {{rot.nsr_ptbxl.diagnosis}}. Per-label calibration repairs the gap at home on all five corpora, {{rot.coverage.mondrian_home_coverage_diagnosis_mean}} the diagnosis {{rot.coverage.mondrian_home_coverage_mean}}.

Away, the rotation holds {{rot.cells.ordered_pairs}}, and {{rot.cells.away_cells}} once the diagnoses are counted separately. Under pooled calibration, coverage over all cases and within the diagnosis {{rot.coverage.none_away_coverage_mean}} {{rot.coverage.none_away_coverage_diagnosis_mean}} acting on top of a gap that was already there. Per-label calibration, which repairs the gap at home, {{rot.coverage.mondrian_away_coverage_diagnosis_mean}} away.

Both of those per-label figures, at home and away, include the three source-diagnosis pairs that cover by declining to answer; over the pairs whose per-class threshold was finite, home and away {{rot.coverage.mondrian_finite_pair}}, and it is the second figure that describes the scheme answering rather than abstaining. Per diagnosis the mean away bias {{rot.bias.AF_away_bias}}, {{rot.bias.RBBB_away_bias}}, {{rot.bias.NSR_away_bias}} that class carries. The spread across sources is larger than any mean: its standard deviation {{rot.bias.sd_range}} atrioventricular block {{rot.bias.sd_worst}}. After the worst pair of section 3.2, PTB-XL's left bundle-branch block threshold spent on CPSC comes {{rot.bias.second_worst}} points. Both of those thresholds were finite in every draw. At home the scheme sits {{rot.bias.home_nsr}} on sinus rhythm and over-covers {{rot.bias.home_others}} on the other four.

A pooled threshold is a quantile of the whole calibration sample and is finite in {{rot.coverage.pooled_cells}}: {{rot.cells.away_n}} away readings, {{rot.cells.home_n}} by a corpus on its own held-out records, and {{rot.cells.holdout_n}} on the calibration part held back from fitting, so no pooled coverage in the rotation comes from abstaining. A per-label threshold can starve.

On Shandong's left bundle-branch block the per-label threshold is {{rot.starved.sph_lbbb}}, on its first-degree {{rot.starved.sph_iavb}}, and on Chapman-Shaoxing with Ningbo's {{rot.starved.chapman_lbbb}}: too few calibration cases of the label for the 90th percentile of their scores to fall below the maximum, so the rule admits both labels and coverage reads high without the scheme separating them. Their sets {{rot.starved.starved_sizes}} of a possible two, {{rot.starved.clean_size}}, and their coverage {{rot.starved.starved_coverage}}. Removing them moves left bundle-branch block {{rot.starved.LBBB_finite}} where the threshold was finite, a change of sign, and first-degree atrioventricular {{rot.starved.IAVB_finite}}. Both columns are in `results/rotation.json`.

Figure 4 rings the pairs whose per-class threshold ran to infinity in some draws, so that their coverage there comes from admitting both labels: {{rot.abstention_by_correction.caption_mondrian}} calibration {{rot.abstention_by_correction.caption_weighted}}, which is why the height of the weighted panel is not a measure of that scheme answering. The figure draws the home and away readings and not the calibration holdout, so one further weighted pair, {{rot.abstention_by_correction.unringed_pair}} and carries no ring. Counted over every role, under per-label calibration {{rot.limitations.mondrian_pairs}} starve; under label-shift weighting, which fits within the label and then {{rot.limitations.weighted_pairs}}. The headline per-label coverages are given with those pairs and without; the Chow and uncertainty medians include them, and the Chow maximum sits on them. No weighted mean is quoted.

At Chongqing, with PTB-XL as source, infarction coverage under pooled calibration {{rot.target_scale.rung_zero}}, measured on the {{ts.n_eval}} tracings held out for evaluation ({{s.none.acs.mi}} over the whole cohort), and recalibrating on 100 of them {{rot.target_scale.recalibrated_100}}, where 500 and 2,000 {{rot.target_scale.recalibrated_tail}}. Pooling the same records with the source calibration sample instead {{rot.target_scale.pooled}} over the same ladder.

At the three infarction sites, Chow's rule with one empirical quantile per class reproduces per-label calibration on both labels at once: infarction coverage within {{chow.ptbxl.mi}}, {{chow.sph.mi}} and {{chow.acs.mi}} points of it at PTB-XL, Shandong and Chongqing, non-infarction coverage within {{chow.ptbxl.non}}, {{chow.sph.non}} and {{chow.acs.non}}, at a refusal rate lower by under a point.

The spread over calibration draws and the bootstrap over the target cohort are different quantities, and the rotation shows which dominates. A bootstrap width is a 95% interval and a draw spread a standard deviation, so the second is put on the first's scale, and the two corrections are read apart. {{rot.uncertainty.pairs_compared}} of `results/rotation_uncertainty.csv`, per-label calibration has a {{rot.uncertainty.mondrian_widths}}; pooled calibration {{rot.uncertainty.none_widths}}. The per-label draw moves more because its threshold is a quantile of one label's calibration cases, the smallest sample in the design. One quantity is what the calibration sample could have been and the other what the cohort could have been, and a receiving site has to read both. {{rot.uncertainty.thin_rows}} {{rot.uncertainty.rows}} rest on {{rot.sizes.thin}} of the diagnosis and are flagged rather than dropped.

Chow's rule places one empirical quantile per class, so the per-label column is the like-for-like comparison, and {{rot.uncertainty.chow_pairs}} the two constructions differ by a {{rot.uncertainty.chow_median}} and {{rot.uncertainty.chow_max}}. At the source the difference is {{aux.correction_points}} of a coverage point, the size of the finite-sample correction, and the rule is the per-label construction minus that correction, so the difference is the correction itself. Across five corpora it is about {{w.rot.chow_times}} times the source-site figure, because the per-class calibration samples are smaller than PTB-XL's {{d.minority_calibration_n}} infarctions, and {{low:rot.chow_outliers.chow_outliers}} whose conformal threshold is infinite, where the (n+1) rank runs past the largest score and the plain quantile does not. Per-label tuning still does most of the work, the conformal apparatus still adds only the correction and the vocabulary, and the correction counts for more where a label is rare.

Over the rotation the plain reject rule of section 4 sits further from the per-diagnosis scheme: the {{rot.discussion.chow}}, about {{w.rot.chow_times}} times what it is worth at the source, because the rotation's per-class samples are smaller. A symmetric reject rule, one that refuses a band around a single threshold, does not reproduce the infarction results: widened until it refuses as much as the per-diagnosis scheme, it takes infarction coverage at the source to {{chow.ptbxl.sym_mi}} and non-infarction coverage to {{chow.ptbxl.sym_non}}, and at Chongqing reads {{chow.acs.sym_mi}} and {{chow.acs.sym_non}} against {{chow.acs.conf_mi}} and {{chow.acs.conf_non}}, because it has one threshold to move. At the source the finite-sample correction is worth {{aux.correction_points}} of a coverage point against a between-draw standard deviation of {{aux.between_draw_sd}} points.

Five encoders were compared for infarction: each was frozen, a linear probe fitted on its PTB-XL representations and the thresholds spent as in section 3.2, {{rot.arms.arms_target}} used elsewhere. All five hold the target at home, {{rot.arms.arms_at_home}}. None reaches it at Chongqing, where {{rot.arms.arms_at_chongqing}}, and {{rot.arms.arms_at_shandong}}. Their discrimination spans {{rot.arms.random_init_auroc}} {{rot.arms.best_auroc}}, both ends of that range being arms with no corpus of this study in their pre-training: the randomly initialised control and the strongest pretrained encoder. Every Chongqing figure is a held-out reading, {{rot.arms.chongqing_held_out}}. The middle of the range cannot be read, since {{rot.arms.contaminated}}, one PTB-XL, one PTB-XL and Shandong together, and one Chapman-Shaoxing with Ningbo, so their PTB-XL AUROCs are not held-out figures and the five cannot be put in an order.

## Appendix G. Coverage inside sex and age

Coverage inside sex and age was measured on the same draws and schemes, in bands wide enough that both labels appear in every one. PTB-XL records sex as male or female and stores every age above 89 as 300 for privacy [9], so those records sit in the oldest band. Subgroup intervals come from a separate bootstrap of 2,000 replicates, each resampling the patients of fold 10 before halving them and refitting every threshold, and a difference between two subgroups is formed inside each replicate, so its interval is on the paired difference. `scripts/subgroups.py` writes `results/subgroups.json`, and a test recomputes all {{w.subgroup_cells}} of its cells from the raw scores without importing it.

The guarantee per-label calibration delivers is conditional on the label, and nothing in it holds within a subgroup of a label. Table G1 gives what the scheme returns to each sex and age band at the source, within each label.

The under-50 infarction row rests on {{sg.young_mi_n}} cases, about {{w.sg.young_mi_per_draw}} per draw, and its upper limit is the ceiling the bootstrap can reach rather than an estimate.

Across age, coverage over all cases falls from {{sg.perlabel.young.all}} under 50 to {{sg.perlabel.old.all}} at 75 and over, a gap of {{sgd.age.all}} points, interval {{sgd.age.all_ci}}, and all of it sits in the non-infarction label, {{sg.perlabel.young.non}} to {{sg.perlabel.old.non}}, a fall of {{sgd.age.non}} points, interval {{sgd.age.non_ci}}. Within infarction, coverage runs the other way, {{sg.perlabel.young.mi}} to {{sg.perlabel.old.mi}}, a difference of {{sgd.age.mi}} points whose interval, {{sgd.age.mi_ci_comma}}, settles nothing. The figure over all cases also mixes in a change of composition, infarction prevalence in the fold rising from {{sg.young_prevalence}} under 50 to {{sg.old_prevalence}} at 75 and over. So the scheme over-calls infarction in the old: {{sg.old_flagged}} of non-infarction patients aged 75 and over are labelled infarction, against {{sg.young_flagged}} under 50.

Across sex, per-label calibration narrows a gap that pooled calibration opens, and on this cohort neither the gap nor its repair is established. Under pooled calibration, coverage of infarctions is {{sg.pooled.men.mi}} in men and {{sg.pooled.women.mi}} in women, a difference of {{sgd.sex.pooled}} points whose interval, {{sgd.sex.pooled_ci_comma}}, sits at zero's edge: it is one of {{w.sg.differences}} paired differences in the file, and an earlier calibration path on the same scores put it at −0.2 to 22.6. Per-label calibration brings the same difference to {{sgd.sex.perlabel}} points, interval {{sgd.sex.perlabel_ci_comma}}. Fold 10 cannot settle either claim, holding {{sg.women_mi_n}} female infarctions of which each draw scores about half.
